H.264 is the most compatible and the lightest to upload. Best when getting footage off the device matters most.
HEVC 10-bit holds far more tonal detail than H.264 at a similar size, and still uploads live. The best balance for evidence you also want to grade.

Mastering records at a very high, fixed bit rate for maximum picture quality — far heavier than HEVC, and the closest thing on Android to the iOS build\'s ProRes tier (Android has no ProRes encoder at all, on any device). Recordings never leave this phone: they\'re too large to upload live, so this trades away the protection the rest of the app is built on — footage surviving because it left the device during the encounter. Choose Mastering when picture quality matters more than that.

A package contains a PDF report, the manifest.json it describes, and the time-stamp proof where one was obtained. It contains no video: the footage stays wherever you already keep it.

Your recordings and their proofs are kept either way. Pro adds the report that turns them into something an attorney or an editor can read.
Tap the orange upload count on the main screen. That shows the queue itself: every piece still waiting, how far the current one has got, and what has already arrived.

The most common cause by far is a storage account with no room left. Witness cannot create the session folder, and everything stops behind it. Free up space, or connect a different account, and the queue starts moving again on its own — nothing is lost while it waits.

The next most common cause is the connection. Pieces upload one at a time so that each one finishes, and when the network is struggling a small preview copy of each piece goes up first. A folder holding previews is not a failure; the full-quality files follow and replace them.
Open Settings and check that “Save recordings to gallery” is switched on. It only affects recordings made after you turn it on.
After a long recording, give it a moment: the pieces are combined the instant you stop, so it should appear within a few seconds.

Because a single continuous file cannot be uploaded until it has finished. If the phone is taken during an encounter, a recording made that way goes with it. Pieces start leaving this phone after fifteen seconds.

Witness puts them back together for you: one video per camera into your gallery, and, when “Combine into one video per camera” is on in Settings, one into your cloud folder as well — but only once every individual piece is already confirmed safe.

Uploads carry on when Witness is closed, at Android\'s own pace. Opening Witness on Wi-Fi and leaving it on screen is the fastest way to clear a backlog. Nothing in the queue expires, and it survives restarting the phone — a piece waits until it is delivered.

Every 15 seconds Witness closes the piece it is writing and starts a new one, so the recording is never held hostage by a file that has not finished. Whatever has already uploaded is beyond the reach of the phone entirely.

Recording itself keeps running even with the app closed or the screen off — it only stops if the phone is switched off, or the recording is force-stopped from Android\'s own app settings. At worst you lose the few seconds that were still being written when that happened.
Not through this app. There is no delete button anywhere in Witness, and it only ever adds files to your storage account.

The real risk is different: somebody holding your unlocked phone could sign in to your storage account through that provider\'s own app or website and delete the footage there. That is worth guarding against in advance.

That already finished the recording. Witness treats the app closing — force-quit, a lock screen, the phone dying — exactly like pressing stop: whatever was already uploaded is safe, and the rest resumes the moment you reopen Witness. Recording keeps running in the background here, unlike on iPhone, so the app closing rarely cuts a recording short at all.
So reopen Witness now. Check the main screen: if an upload count is showing, that recording is on its way. Then look in your cloud folder and gallery, below.

Still not there? Witness keeps every piece privately on this phone until your storage confirms it — nothing is deleted automatically — but that storage is not reachable through a file manager the way a normal folder is, so email us (below) rather than trying to browse for it yourself.
Closed the app, or the phone locked, before you pressed stop?
Tap the people icon at the top of the main screen and start a crew. Others join by scanning your code in Witness, or opening the link you send. iPhone and Android phones can be in the same crew.

Every phone keeps uploading to its own cloud, and each recording\'s folder is shared with the crew\'s emails. Android phones match their clock to network time, so every angle lines up. Phones aren\'t connected live: swap codes before and after recording so everyone knows who and what is in the crew.
Afterwards, open the crew and tap “Make multicam edit files” for Final Cut, Premiere or DaVinci Resolve.
Uploaded while you film, in 15-second pieces, one at a time. Each session gets its own folder named after the date, time and place.
One video per camera for each session, saved to a Witness folder in your gallery, if “Save recordings to gallery” is on in Settings.
Say roughly when you recorded, which storage account you were using, and whether “Save recordings to gallery” was on. A photo of the upload queue screen helps most of all.
Nothing is given up on. If a recording cannot reach your storage or your gallery, it stays on this phone until it can.

It removes its own copy of a piece of footage only after your storage account has confirmed that the piece arrived. If a recording cannot be saved anywhere yet, it stays on this phone and Witness tries again every time you open the app.

Also save a copy of each recording, and of the selfie camera\'s video when it is recording, with faces and licence plates blurred, ready to post without exposing bystanders. Detection runs entirely on this phone and nothing is uploaded to analyse it. It is automatic and can miss a face turned away or a plate at a steep angle, so check the copy before publishing. Your original recording is never changed.
Read back from the camera itself, not from the settings above. If HDR is switched on but the camera didn\'t deliver 10-bit, this says which step didn\'t take.

Turns a finished recording into a PDF report with its timeline, hashes and verification steps, alongside the manifest and time-stamp proof it describes.
Records with the wider tonal range 10-bit HDR captures, for more latitude when grading in post. Unlock Witness Pro to use it.
10-bit HDR needs the HEVC or Mastering codec.
Records with the wider tonal range 10-bit HDR captures, for more latitude when grading in post.
On. Footage keeps more shadow and highlight detail than standard 8-bit, at the cost of a heavier file.
This device can\'t record 10-bit HDR — its camera doesn\'t report HLG10 support. Every other setting on this page still works.

Also produce a shorter cut of the rear camera\'s video with the quiet dead air trimmed out and the stretches where someone is actually talking kept — in addition to, never instead of, the full recording you already get. Meant for sharing something watchable without asking someone to sit through the whole thing. Adds to how long the recording takes to finish assembling afterward.
Unlocked by your one-time purchase. There is nothing to renew or cancel.
Witness Pro is active. Manage or cancel it in your Play Store subscriptions.

When recording both cameras, also produce one video with the front camera as a small inset over the rear one — in addition to, never instead of, the two separate videos you already get. Meant for sharing a single file rather than two. Adds noticeably to how long the recording takes to finish assembling afterward.
Witness Pro features: 4K at 60 fps with 10-bit HDR, stabilization from off to extreme, both cameras in one video, blurred faces and plates, and highlight cuts.
Both cameras at once is limited to 1080p, 30 fps, H.264 and 8-bit. Anything above that takes priority and only the rear camera records.

Record a landscape 16:9 video while holding the phone upright, the way you\'d hold it for a call or a text. Witness uses the camera\'s taller 4:3 frame and keeps a landscape strip from the middle, often 1920 × 1080 or better. The viewfinder shows exactly that strip. Single camera only, so the front camera pauses while it\'s on; not available with 10-bit HDR. With the phone held on its side, recording is normal.

What the Play Store returned when this app last asked for its products. A product that has not been activated, or that belongs to a release track this build did not come from, is simply absent from the reply rather than an error — which otherwise looks exactly like a missing button.

Burns the date, time and coordinates into the picture itself, visible to anyone who watches the video — for outlets that want dashcam-style on-screen provenance. This is separate from the invisible metadata every recording already carries, on or off: the SHA-256 hash, the chain-of-custody manifest, and the independent RFC 3161 timestamp. Turning this off doesn\'t remove any of that. Not available together with 10-bit HDR.
Built for documentary and investigative work. Everything in the free app stays free, Pro only adds capture quality.
Witness Pro unlocks 4K, higher frame rates, and 10-bit HDR — and helps fund the app. %1$s
Voice disguise pitches voices down and reshapes their tone so speakers are hard to recognise while words stay clear. It deters ordinary listeners, not specialist analysis.
Recording fills storage at this rate. Witness keeps recording when space runs low, but the device will eventually stop it.

Create a Google account used only for Witness, and sign in to it here. Crucially, do not add that account to your phone\'s system accounts, the Gmail or Drive apps, or any browser you\'re signed into. Then there is no way to open that Drive from your phone to delete anything, the account simply isn\'t reachable through the phone\'s apps. This app keeps its own private login and offers no way to view or delete the footage.

Create a %1$s account used only for Witness, and sign in to it here. Crucially, do not add that account to your phone\'s system accounts, any of that provider\'s apps, or any browser you\'re signed into. Then there is no way to open that account from your phone to delete anything, it simply isn\'t reachable through the phone\'s apps. This app keeps its own private login and offers no way to view or delete the footage.

Your footage uploads to your own %1$s account. There, the account owner can always delete their files. So if someone has your unlocked phone and can open the %1$s app or its website — or, for Google, Gmail too, since it shares the same sign-in — they can delete the recordings there, and deleting them removes access for your emergency contacts too.

Sharing with an emergency contact does not, by itself, give them a separate copy: it grants them a view of your file. If your copy is deleted, their view disappears with it (though deleted files usually sit in a trash/recently-deleted folder for a while first, unless that is also emptied).

These steps are optional. If you\'d rather use your everyday Google account, Witness still works exactly the same, this only affects how hard it is for someone with your phone to delete footage after the fact.

These steps are optional. If you\'d rather use your everyday account, Witness still works exactly the same, this only affects how hard it is for someone with your phone to delete footage after the fact.
Have contacts keep their own copy

When an emergency contact receives the shared folder, they can open it and choose “Make a copy” to save the footage into their own Drive. That copy belongs to them and cannot be deleted from your phone or account.
When an emergency contact receives the shared folder, they can save their own copy of the footage into their own account. That copy belongs to them and cannot be deleted from your phone or account.

Your footage uploads to your own Google Drive. In Google Drive, the account owner can always delete their files. So if someone has your unlocked phone and can open the Google Drive app, the Gmail app, or drive.google.com in a browser, they can delete the recordings there, and deleting them removes access for your emergency contacts too.

Sharing with an emergency contact does not, by itself, give them a separate copy: it grants them a view of your file. If your copy is deleted, their view disappears with it (though deleted files sit in Drive\'s Trash, recoverable for ~30 days, unless the Trash is also emptied).

Use credentials on that server dedicated to Witness (an app password, where the server offers one) rather than your main account password, and don\'t sign in to that same server from apps on this phone. Then there\'s no way to reach it from the phone to delete anything.

Your footage uploads to the server you configured. Anyone who can sign in to that server — through its own web interface, another app, or a different device — can delete files there, the same as with any account. WebDAV has no sharing feature, so emergency contacts are never granted a view to lose in the first place.
Witness never deletes your recordings, there is no delete button anywhere in this app, and it only ever adds files to your storage account.
Confirmed by your storage — these are on it now, not on their way.
Confirmed by your storage. The separate pieces have been replaced there by one video per camera, which is why the folder holds fewer files than the count above.
Pieces upload one at a time, oldest first, so each one finishes instead of all of them crawling together. Nothing is deleted from this phone until your storage confirms it arrived.

Small preview copies go up straight away, without waiting behind the full piece they stand in for. Full pieces go one at a time, oldest first, so each one finishes instead of all of them crawling together. Nothing is deleted from this phone until your storage confirms it arrived.

Each item below lists the SHA-256 of what was captured and whether an independent RFC 3161 time-stamp proof exists for it. Details and notes were written afterwards by the person who made the recording and are not part of the hashed record.
To check any item, drop its files together with the .json record and .tsr proof shared with this report into witnesscamera.com/verify. It runs in the browser and uploads nothing.
Imported: the proof starts when the file was imported, not when it was made.

Turning this off never stops an upload already under way. Anything filmed while it was on keeps going until your storage confirms it, and no setting in this app can call that back — so taking the phone and switching this off cannot unsend what has already been recorded.

On, every recording is sent to your storage as you film. Off, new recordings stay on this phone only — still recorded, still hashed and timestamped, and saved to your gallery, which becomes the only place they exist.

When a recording starts uploading, each contact with an email is granted view access to that recording\'s cloud folder and notified by email. They can watch footage arrive live, access that survives even if your phone is taken. Contacts are only shared with when you record.

\n\nDuring a recording, a location button lets you send your last known location to every contact here by text and email, whichever they have on file — you send it yourself from a compose screen, nothing goes out automatically.

%s can\'t grant access automatically: emergency contacts with an email won\'t be notified or given access to your recordings. Switch to a provider that supports sharing, or share a folder yourself from that account.

Once every small chunk of a session is safely uploaded, Witness merges them into a single video per camera, uploads that to the session\'s Drive folder, and then deletes the small chunks, so you get one clean file per camera instead of a folder full of pieces. This never happens until the small chunks are already confirmed in Drive, so nothing is at risk while it runs. Turn this off to keep the individual chunks instead.
Both cameras are off because of: %1$s.
Recording both cameras at once is limited to 1080p, 30 fps and H.264, and can\'t do 10-bit HDR. Change these in Witness Pro, or restore them here and the front camera switches back on by itself.
Both cameras need the free capture settings

Records the front (selfie) camera at the same time as the rear one, producing two synchronized videos per session. Android caps simultaneous two-camera capture at 720p per camera; single-camera recordings stay at 1080p. Uses more battery and may warm the device during long recordings.
This device can\'t record both cameras simultaneously, so only the rear camera is used.

Placeholders: {date}, {time}, {location}, {session}. Each recording session\'s Drive subfolder is named from this template. Only applies to sessions started after you change it, existing folders keep their names.

Saves one stitched video per camera per recording session into a Witness folder in your gallery, as backup independent of Google Drive. If you sync your gallery to a cloud photo service, it goes there too. Turn this off to keep recordings out of your gallery, Drive upload is unaffected.
Held on because nothing is uploading these recordings — with cloud upload off, or in the Mastering codec, the gallery is the only place they exist. Your own setting comes back when uploading resumes.
Add the Witness tile to Quick Settings, or the Witness widget to your home screen, to start recording in one tap. You can also say \"Hey Google, start recording with Witness\".

Android reserves the power-button double-press for camera apps, so turning this on also offers Witness as a camera app and Android will ask which one to use. Turn it off to give the gesture back to your usual camera.
Recordings start at the 0.5× ultra-wide lens when the device supports it, otherwise 1×.
With the viewfinder on you can switch 0.5×↔1× live while recording, with no gap in the footage.
Recordings start at the 0.5× ultra-wide lens. In dual-camera mode, if the device can\'t run 0.5× with the front camera, it records a single 0.5× camera rather than switching to 1×.
Recordings start at the standard 1× lens.
Send a stand-in when uploads fall behind

When uploads are visibly falling behind, Witness sends a small, low-quality copy of each new chunk ahead of the full-quality file, so something arrives fast even on a struggling connection. The full file follows and replaces it as soon as the network allows. Off by default costs nothing on a healthy connection: the stand-in is only ever produced when it\'s actually needed.
Not signed in, sign in from the home screen.
Witness never deletes your recordings from cloud storage itself. But anyone holding your unlocked phone could delete them through that account\'s own app or website. Learn how to guard against that.
Black keeps the screen dark while recording; triple-tap it for the controls, then tap the eye to see the camera. Show camera opens straight into the viewfinder.

Burns the date, time and coordinates into the picture itself, visible to anyone who watches the video. This is separate from the invisible metadata every recording already carries, on or off: the SHA-256 hash, the chain-of-custody manifest, and the independent RFC 3161 timestamp.
It also reads \"Recorded with Witness\". Witness Pro leaves only the time and place.
Switched off while 10-bit HDR is on.

With the viewfinder on, recording starts with a live preview instead of a black screen. You can also toggle it any time while recording.

On Nextcloud or ownCloud, the address is under Settings, then WebDAV. Use an app password rather than your account password where the server offers one: it can be revoked on its own if this phone is lost.

Emergency contacts can\'t be given access automatically on WebDAV: the protocol has no sharing feature, and each server adds its own. Everything else works the same, and you can still share a folder yourself from your server.
